analysis.one_liner: Makes private equity funds liable for debts of companies they take over and taxes carried interest as ordinary income.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made private equity funds and their partners legally responsible for the debts, pension obligations, and legal penalties of the companies they buy and control. It would have barred those funds from paying themselves dividends or buying back shares from an acquired company for two years after the takeover, moved workers' unpaid wages, severance, and benefits ahead of other creditors in bankruptcy, restricted executive bonuses in bankruptcy cases, and required funds to disclose fees and returns and act in investors' interests. It also would have ended the carried-interest tax break, taxing private equity managers' profit shares as ordinary income instead of at lower capital-gains rates.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies owned by private equity funds, who would get first claim on unpaid wages, severance, and benefits in bankruptcy and new ways to recover money taken out of a failing company. Pension fund beneficiaries and other investors would get fee and performance disclosures and fiduciary protections. Taxpayers would gain revenue from taxing carried interest as ordinary income, and gift card holders would get priority for unredeemed balances in a bankruptcy.

how_it_helps.text: Makes a private equity fund and its partners jointly liable for all debts of any company it acquires and controls, including pension withdrawal liabilities and penalties under worker-notice and labor laws, so failed companies' obligations do not simply vanish.

Bars an acquired company from paying dividends, buybacks, or similar distributions to the fund for two years after the takeover, and lets employees and creditors sue to claw back transfers made in violation, with attorney's fees awarded.
Doubles the priority wage claim in bankruptcy to $20,000 per worker and adds priority for severance pay and for contributions owed to employee health and welfare plans.

Restricts executive bonuses and retention pay in bankruptcy, blocks special compensation if the company cut severance for rank-and-file workers in the prior year, and requires courts to weigh job preservation when approving sales of a bankrupt company.
Taxes carried interest, the profit share private equity and other fund managers receive, as ordinary income rather than at lower capital-gains rates.
Requires funds to disclose fees and returns, imposes fiduciary obligations toward investors, and bars funds from forcing investors to waive those duties.
Gives gift card holders a priority claim of up to $1,800 for unredeemed balances when a retailer goes bankrupt.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity fund managers and their partners, who would bear personal liability for portfolio-company debts, lose the ability to extract dividends and fees from newly acquired companies for two years, pay a surtax on certain payments from companies they control, and pay ordinary income tax rates on carried interest. Critics also warn the cost would reach buyout targets if funds stop purchasing struggling companies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity fund managers and partners

drawbacks.text: The bill makes a fund jointly liable for every debt of any company it controls, not just failing ones, which could make funds unwilling to buy distressed or struggling companies and shrink the pool of capital available to turn them around.

The surtax on payments from acquired companies and tighter limits on deducting business interest would sharply raise the cost of leveraged buyouts, and critics of the approach argue that could push deal structures offshore or reduce buyout activity overall.

The two-year dividend ban applies to every acquisition regardless of whether the deal succeeds, so well-run investments that return capital to investors would face the same restriction as the failed takeovers the bill targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker and bankruptcy protections address a real gap: today, fund managers can collect fees and dividends from a company that later fails, while employees lose wages, severance, and pensions. The carried-interest change raises revenue from a narrow, wealthy group. The tradeoff is real, though: blanket liability for all portfolio-company debts and a flat two-year dividend ban are blunt tools that could deter legitimate turnarounds as well as value-stripping, and the bill's sweeping design is one reason it drew industry opposition and little movement in committee even among allies.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, a Senate Banking Committee hearing touched on private equity a year later, but no committee ever voted on the bill and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on October 20, 2021, joined by Senators Baldwin, Brown, Sanders, and Merkley.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance that same day; no further committee or floor action on the bill followed.
On September 8, 2022, the Banking Committee held a hearing on the subject and printed it as S.Hrg. 117-747, but that hearing was not a markup or vote on the bill.
No vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds and their managers are better off: they kept the current rules, with no added liability for portfolio-company debts, no limits on extracting dividends from acquired companies, and carried interest still taxed at capital-gains rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity funds and their managers

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Wall Street Looting Act and assembled its four cosponsors.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, and his Banking Committee held a hearing on private equity printed as S.Hrg. 117-747.

for.name: Tammy Baldwin, Jeff Merkley, and Bernie Sanders
for.role: 3 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.role: U.S. Senator (D-OR), chair of the Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill as Finance Committee chair and never scheduled a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the 117th Congress.

against.name: Private equity industry
against.role: Fund managers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill, arguing its liability and tax provisions would damage the industry and the companies it invests in.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats plus one independent who caucuses with them; no Republican cosponsored, and the Senate never held a vote that would have shown the parties' split.

industries.industry: Private equity funds and buyout fund managers
industries.note: The bill would impose joint and several liability for portfolio-company debts and pension liabilities, ban dividends and buybacks from acquired firms for two years, levy a surtax on payments extracted from them, and limit interest deductions. Because the bill died, the industry kept all of these rules.

industries.industry: Carried-interest recipients (private equity, real estate, and hedge fund partners)
industries.note: The bill would tax managers' profit shares as ordinary income rather than at lower capital-gains rates, a direct cost to the highest-earning fund partners. The break remained in place.
The bill requires funds to disclose fees and returns, imposes fiduciary duties, and specifically shields pension funds from the new control-person liability, protecting retirement savers' money.

The bill would treat unpaid wages and benefit contributions as costs recoverable from the collateral securing lenders' claims, putting employee pay ahead of lender recovery. This provision never took effect.
